title: Hoctor v. USDA (1996)
summary: A rule that fixes a specific number an agency could not derive by interpretation from its statute or regulation is a legislative rule that must go through notice and comment, so an eight foot fence requirement announced in an internal memorandum was invalid.
notes:
Key line: "There is no way to reason to an eight-foot perimeter-fence rule as opposed to a seven-and-a-half foot fence or a nine-foot fence or a ten-foot fence." (Posner, C.J.)

Citation: 82 F.3d 165 (7th Cir. 1996).

sections.Parties: The petitioner was Patrick D. Hoctor, a small licensed dealer in exotic animals who kept lions, tigers, ligers, cougars and snow leopards on a 25 acre compound outside Terre Haute, Indiana. The respondent was the United States Department of Agriculture, which had sanctioned him under the Animal Welfare Act of 1966, 7 U.S.C. sections 2131 and following, for failing to have a perimeter fence at least eight feet high. The Department was represented by its Office of General Counsel; Hoctor was represented by a Terre Haute attorney. The case was heard by the Seventh Circuit on a petition for review of the Department's order, with Chief Judge Posner writing for a panel that included Judges Diane Wood and Evans.
sections.Material Facts: The Animal Welfare Act requires the Department to set standards for the humane handling, care, treatment and transportation of animals by dealers, including minimum housing requirements. After notice and comment the Department adopted a structural strength regulation, 9 C.F.R. section 3.125(a), requiring that housing facilities be structurally sound and maintained to protect the animals from injury and to contain them. When Hoctor began dealing in 1982, a Department veterinarian who inspected his farm suggested a six foot perimeter fence, which he built around a compound whose animals were already kept in pens inside a containment fence. In 1983 the Department issued an internal memorandum to its inspectors stating that dangerous animals, including lions, tigers and leopards, must be inside a perimeter fence at least eight feet high and at least three feet from any pen. Beginning in 1990 inspectors cited Hoctor for violating section 3.125(a) because his fence was six feet. Replacing it would cost many thousands of dollars.
sections.Procedural History: The Department brought an administrative enforcement proceeding and sanctioned Hoctor for the fence violation and other alleged violations. Hoctor petitioned the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit for review, limiting his challenge to the perimeter fence requirement. The parties agreed that unless the eight foot rule was a valid interpretive rule, the sanction for violating it was improper. The case was argued on February 9, 1996, and decided on April 25, 1996. The court vacated the order under review because it rested on a rule that was invalid for want of notice and comment.
sections.Issue: Whether the Department's requirement, announced in a 1983 internal memorandum without notice and comment, that dangerous animals be kept inside a perimeter fence at least eight feet high was a valid interpretive rule exempt from the rulemaking requirements of 5 U.S.C. section 553(b)(A) because it interpreted the structural strength regulation, or whether it was a legislative rule that could bind Hoctor only if promulgated after public notice and an opportunity to comment.
sections.Holding: The court held that the eight foot rule was a legislative rule, invalid because the Department had not used notice and comment. A requirement of an eight foot fence cannot be derived from a general duty of secure containment by any process reasonably described as interpretation, because nothing makes eight feet uniquely appropriate compared with seven and a half, nine or ten. When an agency bases a rule on an arbitrary choice among methods of implementation it is legislating, and legislative rules require notice and comment. The order sanctioning Hoctor was vacated. The court assumed without deciding that the Department had statutory authority to require eight foot fences and that containing dangerous animals was a proper concern under the Act.
sections.Reasoning: Chief Judge Posner explained why interpretive rules are exempt from notice and comment: every agency enforcing a less than crystalline statute must interpret it, and the public benefits when interpretations are announced in advance. The structural strength regulation spoke of sturdiness, not height, and the Department's argument that a six foot fence has zero structural strength between six and eight feet was a wonderful lawyer's argument but no more. If the rule were one of the minimum standards the statute directs the Department to create, it could not be interpretive because there would be nothing to interpret; a statute that authorizes an agency to impose a duty makes formulating that duty a legislative task. Even assuming the regulation imposed a general duty of secure containment, interpretation in the narrow sense ascertains meaning, and eight feet is not part of the meaning of secure containment. Rules that turn on a number are usually arbitrary in the sense that they could be different without impairing any regulatory purpose. Such choices are legislative, and notice and comment is the analogue of the legislative process that lets thousands of affected dealers be heard. Interpretive rules can have numerical components where technical criteria or rebuttable rules of thumb tie the number to the underlying standard, as in American Mining Congress, but the eight foot rule was as flat as they come. Courts decide what kind of rule requires notice and comment.
